title: Maintenance Metrics That Prove ROI in a 90-Day Pilot
summary: Which maintenance metrics prove ROI in a 90-day pilot? Five metrics, rules finance trusts, full program cost and a one-page day-90 report template.
body_markdown:
## Key Points


- A pilot that gets the rollout funded shows confirmed findings with an agreed dollar value, set against the program's full cost.
- Savings only count if someone outside maintenance can audit them, under rules set before the pilot starts.
- [Total cost of ownership](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/total-cost-of-ownership) sets the full program cost against what manual routes and emergency repairs cost today.


When finance approves a predictive maintenance business case, the yes is often to a pilot, not a full rollout: a limited set of assets, a fixed window and a review at the end. That review decides whether the full rollout gets funded, and the maintenance metrics in your report are what it decides on.


Pilots often fail that review even when the system works and the team likes it. The report says the pilot went well, but finance funds a number it agreed to measure before the pilot started.


## Which maintenance metrics prove ROI to finance?


Five maintenance metrics prove ROI to finance: confirmed findings, agreed value per finding, downtime hours avoided, share of emergency work orders, and program cost to date. Each one connects to money and traces back to a record finance can check. Here is what each means in a pilot:


- **Confirmed findings:** failures or developing faults the system flagged and your team verified on the asset.
- **Agreed value per finding:** what each confirmed finding is worth, based on rules finance signed off on before the pilot started.
- **Downtime hours avoided:** the stops that didn't happen because a finding was acted on in time.
- **Share of emergency work orders:** how much of your work is still reactive, compared with your baseline.
- **Program cost to date:** everything the pilot has cost so far, not just the invoice.


Confirmed findings and avoided hours both depend on alerts turning into work on the floor. In a[Verdantix study commissioned by Tractian](https://tractian.com/en/resources/reports/verdantix) , 80% of the 60 maintenance, operations and reliability leaders surveyed said translating alerts into maintenance action is a significant challenge.


Technical pilot metrics, vendor requirements and pilot scope sit one step earlier in the chain. Learn more about[testing AI predictive maintenance software in 90 days](https://tractian.com/en/blog/what-to-require-from-ai-predictive-maintenance-software-and-how-to-prove-it-in-90-days) .


## How do you make savings numbers finance trusts?


Agree the rules with finance before day one: the cost of downtime, what counts as a finding, how avoided hours are estimated, how production value is reported and who signs off. Savings figures get questioned when nobody agreed where the numbers came from. In the same Verdantix survey, 82% of leaders pointed to integration gaps with their CMMS or EAM systems, and a saving is hard to audit when the finding and the repair sit in different systems.


The five rules:


- **Agree the hourly**[cost of downtime](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/cost-of-downtime) **with finance.** Use the figure from your business case, and get finance to confirm it in writing. If finance set the number, it is harder to dispute at day 90.
- **Count only confirmed findings.** An alert isn't a saving. A finding counts when someone inspected the asset and confirmed the fault.
- **Use conservative avoided hours.** For each finding, estimate the downtime it prevented on the low side, and write down why.
- **Report production value on its own line.** Keep production savings separate from maintenance savings so each one can be checked. Tate & Lyle does this in its[published results](https://tractian.com/en/case-studies/cpkelco) : $446.9K in total cost savings at its San Diego facility, including $380K in production uptime.
- **Name who signs off.** Pick one person outside maintenance, usually in finance or operations, who reviews and approves each saving as it comes in.


Check the payback against the model manufacturer in the Verdantix ROI research, which reached break-even in 8 months. If your projected payback is far shorter or longer, be ready to explain why.


These rules are easier to follow when findings, actions and avoided downtime are recorded in one place as they happen. Tractian[downtime prevention and reporting](https://tractian.com/en/solutions/downtime-prevention) records alerts and fixes as they happen and reports them as downtime avoided, savings, MTBF and ROI.


## What does a condition monitoring program really cost?


A condition monitoring program's cost includes the sensors and everything needed to run them. A total cost of ownership (TCO) view adds hardware, subscription, installation, connectivity, team time to act on alerts and training, and together they make up the predictive maintenance cost. The components:


- **Hardware:** sensors and any gateways they need.
- **Subscription:** the software and analytics, usually billed yearly.
- **Installation:** mounting sensors and setting up assets in the system.
- **Connectivity:** how data gets off the plant floor. Ask whether this needs an IT project, because that adds time and internal cost.
- **Team time to act on alerts:** someone has to review findings, plan the work and close the loop.
- **Training:** getting technicians and planners comfortable with the new workflow.


Then set that against what you spend today on the same job: manual inspection routes, outsourced vibration analysis, and the emergency repairs that slip through anyway.


Route labor belongs in that comparison. The hours your team spends walking routes and collecting readings are a real cost even when they never appear on an invoice, so count them next to the subscription.

## Which assets and how long?


Run the pilot for 90 days on[critical assets](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/critical-assets) with a failure history. Critical assets give each finding a real cost to weigh against, and a failure history makes it likely that findings show up inside the window. A pilot on assets that rarely fail can run perfectly and still have nothing to show at day 90.


Use the 12 months of events from your problem statement to choose. The assets that failed most often, or cost the most when they did, are the ones most likely to produce findings worth reporting.


## What goes in the report to finance at day 90?


The day-90 report is one page that finance can read in a few minutes: pilot scope, confirmed findings, validated value, downtime hours avoided, emergency work orders, cost to date, projection to full rollout and payback. Together they show whether the pilot paid for itself.


Copy this template:


**Pilot scope:** \[number\] assets on \[line or area\], \[start date\] to \[end date\].


**Confirmed findings:** \[number\], each verified on the asset by \[name or team\].


**Validated value:** \[amount\], using the agreed cost of downtime of \[amount per hour\]. Production value: \[amount\]. Maintenance value: \[amount\]. Signed off by \[name, role\].


**Downtime hours avoided:** \[hours\], estimated conservatively.


**Emergency work orders:** \[share\] of total work orders, compared with \[baseline share\] before the pilot.


**Cost to date:** \[amount\], including hardware, subscription, installation and team time.


**Projection to full rollout:** \[number\] assets, with expected value of \[conservative case\] to \[base case\] per year.


**Payback:** \[months\] in the conservative case, \[months\] in the base case.


Each number on that page should trace back to a rule finance agreed to before the pilot started, so the day-90 review checks numbers finance already accepted.


## FAQ


**Is 90 days long enough to prove ROI?**


Usually, on the right assets. Ninety days on critical assets with a failure history is often enough for confirmed findings to show up and be valued. On assets that rarely fail, it may not be, which is why asset selection matters as much as the length of the pilot.


**What counts as a validated saving?**


A saving from a confirmed finding (a fault someone verified on the asset), valued with the downtime cost finance agreed to before the pilot, estimated conservatively and signed off by someone outside maintenance. Anything else is an estimate, and should be reported as one.
